t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this topic we study mechanical asphyxia. Mechanical asphyxia is a disturbance of external respiration under the action of a mechanical factor: oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises. The forensic medical classification distinguishes three types: asphyxia from compression, from closure, and asphyxia in a confined space. Hanging accounts for 65-70% of deaths from asphyxia, while strangulation accounts for more than two thirds of deaths. Plan: hypoxia, the course of asphyxia, the postasphyxial state, general signs, then strangulation, obturation, compression asphyxia and asphyxia in a closed space.

t: Oxygen requirement and intensity of hypoxia
n: Oxygen requirement and intensity of hypoxia. 98.5-99.0% of oxygen is taken in through the respiratory organs, the rest through the skin, stomach and intestines. At rest 6-8 L of air per minute are needed; with physical exertion the requirement sometimes rises 10-20 times. If tissue respiration in the central nervous system stops for 5-10 minutes, the changes are not restored; in muscle and connective tissue this time is considerably longer. By speed, hypoxia is fulminant, acute, subacute or chronic. In forensic medicine the first two are important.

t: Types of exogenous hypoxia
n: Types of exogenous hypoxia. The oxygen in air is normally 20.93%. In the hypoxic form there is less oxygen in the inspired air. By pressure, the following are distinguished: hypobaric, that is, mountain sickness; normobaric, that is, a gas poor in oxygen; hyperbaric, that is, deep water. In the hyperoxic form the oxygen concentration is high, while in the hypercapnic form CO2 rises in a confined space. Attention: hyperoxic and hypercapnic are not the same. In one there is a lot of oxygen, in the other a lot of carbon dioxide.

t: Types of endogenous hypoxia
n: Endogenous hypoxia has five types: respiratory, circulatory, haemic, cytotoxic and physiological. The direct form of the respiratory type is compression of the neck and closure of the airways, while the indirect form is observed in shock and sepsis. Circulatory hypoxia is associated with disturbance of the circulation, and haemic hypoxia with reduction of haemoglobin. In cytotoxic hypoxia, tissue respiration is impaired. Physiological hypoxia is temporary and occurs with physical exertion or when a large amount of food is eaten at once.

t: The concept of asphyxia and mechanical asphyxia
n: The concept of asphyxia and mechanical asphyxia. In forensic medicine, lack of oxygen has long been designated by the term asphyxia. In Greek: a is negation, sphygmos is pulse, that is, absence of pulse. Asphyxia is an acute disturbance of the activity of vital systems, with lack of oxygen and accumulation of carbon dioxide as a result of impaired external respiration. In asphyxia, hypoxia always develops together with hypercapnia. A state arising from impaired external respiration under the action of a mechanical factor is called mechanical asphyxia. Remember: hypoxia and asphyxia are not the same, because in asphyxia hypercapnia is present as well.

t: Classification of mechanical asphyxia
n: Classification of mechanical asphyxia. In the forensic medical classification there are three types of mechanical asphyxia: from compression, from closure, and in a confined space. Asphyxia from compression is divided into two types: strangulation, compression of the neck organs, and compression asphyxia proper, compression of the organs of the chest and abdominal cavities. Asphyxia from closure includes closure of the respiratory orifices, closure of the airways and drowning. In a confined space oxygen falls. A special case is autoasphyxiophilia, that is, sexual asphyxia: sexual arousal takes place under conditions of hypoxia and hypercapnia.

t: Autoasphyxiophilia (sexual asphyxia)
n: In autoasphyxiophilia, that is, sexual or autoerotic asphyxia, sexual arousal takes place under conditions of hypoxia and hypercapnia. Orgasm occurs spontaneously or as a result of masturbation. It is more often observed in lone middle-aged men inclined to sexual deviations, sometimes in young men. The particular feature is that the person controls the asphyxial process himself with the hands, feet or devices; the neck is compressed by a ligature or a polythene bag is put over the head. Sometimes it ends in death and is assessed as an accident. At the scene there may be found pornographic images, imitations of sexual organs, and clothing of the opposite sex.

t: Case analysis 1: suspicious death at the scene
n: Case analysis one: suspicious death at the scene. A teaching example: a lone middle-aged man is found dead in his room. There is a ligature on the neck, tightened not by the weight of the body but by means of a device. At the scene there are pornographic images and imitations of sexual organs; the sexual organs of the corpse are exposed, and signs characteristic of masturbation may be found. There is a risk of error: hanging is most often a method of suicide, whereas death in sexual asphyxia is assessed as an accident. Question: on which evidence will you rely in assessing the kind of death, and what else will you look for at the scene?

t: Quick question 1
n: Quick question one. What are the types of exogenous hypoxia? Hypoxic, hyperoxic and hypercapnic. The types of endogenous hypoxia? Respiratory, haemic, circulatory, cytotoxic and physiological. What is asphyxia? Lack of oxygen and accumulation of carbon dioxide due to impaired external respiration; hypoxia develops together with hypercapnia. The types of mechanical asphyxia? Asphyxia from compression, from closure, and in a confined space.

t: Preasphyxial period of asphyxia
n: The preasphyxial period of asphyxia lasts on average 20-30 seconds. Breathing stops for a short time, then its rhythm slows. Sometimes disorderly movements are observed. The organism tries to overcome the action of the asphyxial factor with its compensatory-adaptive capacities. The amount of oxygen-carrying blood increases, the blood becomes thinner and is redistributed in favour of vital organs. Thanks to this adaptation, signs of asphyxia do not yet develop in this period.

t: Stages of the asphyxial period
n: Stages of the asphyxial period. The inspiratory and expiratory stages last about 1 minute each, and consciousness is usually lost in 40-60 seconds. The stage of respiratory arrest lasts 30-40 seconds, and terminal breathing may continue for up to 5 minutes. After the respiratory centre is paralysed, the heart may beat for another 3-10 minutes. Then the heart stops and clinical death begins. The sequence: inspiratory dyspnoea, expiratory dyspnoea, respiratory arrest, terminal breathing, complete arrest.

t: Inspiratory and expiratory dyspnoea: comparison
n: We compare inspiratory and expiratory dyspnoea. In the inspiratory stage, inspiration quickens and lengthens, pleural pressure falls sharply, arterial pressure falls, venous pressure rises, and the pulse slows. In the expiratory stage, expiration is strong and more prolonged, pleural pressure rises, arterial pressure rises, venous pressure falls, the pulse quickens and clonic convulsions occur. Strong convulsions with passing of urine, semen and faeces are possible. In convulsions, parts of the body strike surrounding objects, and various injuries appear. Remember: convulsive injuries are not injuries inflicted by another person, and they must be distinguished.

t: Terminal stage and reflex cardiac arrest
n: The terminal stage and reflex cardiac arrest. In the terminal stage, the centres of the spinal cord are activated. Occasionally, irregular respiratory movements of varying depth appear, and the mouth often opens. The stage lasts up to 5 minutes. At the end arterial pressure falls greatly, reflexes disappear, and sometimes there are strong convulsions. The respiratory centre is paralysed and breathing stops completely. Attention: respiratory arrest is not equal to cardiac arrest; the heart may beat for another 3-10 minutes. Reflex cardiac arrest is possible: on irritation of the receptors of the carotid sinus, larynx, trachea and bronchi, or on injury to the vagus and superior laryngeal nerves.

t: Case analysis 2: rapid death and absence of signs
n: Case analysis two: rapid death and absence of signs. A hypothetical situation: on the corpse of a person with the neck compressed by a ligature, no asphyxial signs such as cyanosis and Tardieu's spots were found. Question: does this mean that there was no asphyxia? If the heart stops within 30 seconds of the asphyxial action, the general asphyxial signs do not have time to develop. In ligature strangulation the reflexogenic zones of the neck are irritated more, so reflex cardiac arrest is possible before the signs have fully developed. For discussion: in hanging, the strangulation furrow on the neck is the main sign, and the furrow is compared with the ligature.

t: Periods of the postasphyxial state
n: Periods of the postasphyxial state. The first period is asphyxial coma: atony of the muscles, absence of reflexes; then decerebrate rigidity and convulsions. The second period is stupor: consciousness is restored, from sopor to drowsiness. The third period is disorientation and memory impairment: disorientation in time and space is observed, with retrograde amnesia and confabulations. The fourth period is residual effects: in mild cases they pass in 1-2 weeks, and in severe cases memory and attention are impaired.

t: Postasphyxial state: consequences and complications
n: The postasphyxial state: consequences and complications. In mild cases, with full care, the changes disappear without trace in 1-2 weeks. In severe cases memory and attention are impaired, and headache, paralysis and sometimes reduced intelligence remain. Hypoxia leads to dystrophy and necrosis in the liver and to shock changes in the kidneys; in the gastrointestinal tract erosions and ulcers develop, followed by peritonitis or bleeding. In the first minutes and hours death results from asphyxial coma, and in the first day from oedema of the lungs and brain. Later the cause of death is hypostatic pneumonia. In determining the severity of injury in a living person and the cause of death, medical documents with full information are of great importance.

t: General external signs of mechanical asphyxia
n: General external signs of mechanical asphyxia. Attention: cyanosis of the face and neck is not constant. In a corpse lying on its back it may disappear, and when it lies face down the face may be bluish even without asphyxia. The cadaveric lividity is extensive, bluish-violet, and appears rapidly within an hour after death; the reason is the fluid state of the blood and its saturation with carbon dioxide. Small haemorrhages into the conjunctiva of the eyes, that is, subconjunctival ecchymoses, arise in dyspnoea because of the change in pressure. Dilatation of the pupils is not constant. In convulsions, because of contraction of smooth muscle, urine and faeces are passed involuntarily; in a man, semen, and in a woman, the mucous plug of the cervical canal.

t: General internal signs of mechanical asphyxia
n: General internal signs of mechanical asphyxia. Partial emphysema of the lungs appears in the stage of dyspnoea; the internal organs are venous-congested. The signs are non-specific and are found also in other rapid deaths, so in diagnosis their totality is assessed. Four signs are given in the table. The fluid blood in the heart and large veins is dark red. In the asphyxial heart the right chambers are more congested. Tardieu's spots of 2-3 mm are dark red and lie beneath the pleura and epicardium. Sabinsky's sign is an anaemic and contracted spleen; the cause is the discharge of depot blood in the preasphyxial period. The asphyxial heart, anaemia and a contracted spleen are relatively pathognomonic signs.

t: Case analysis 3: the signs are non-specific
n: Case analysis three: the signs are non-specific. Situation: on a corpse, cyanosis of the face, Tardieu's spots and fluid dark red blood were found. Question: does this prove mechanical asphyxia alone? No. These changes are found also in other kinds of rapid death: sudden cardiac death, electrical injury, anaphylactic shock. In diagnosis the signs are assessed not individually but as a totality, that is, together. There is a risk of error: cyanosis is not constant, disappears in the supine position, and in the face-down position may be bluish even without asphyxia.

t: Quick question 2
n: Quick question two. How many seconds on average does the preasphyxial period last? 20-30 seconds; in this period signs of asphyxia do not yet develop. Which stage follows the stage of inspiratory dyspnoea? Expiratory dyspnoea, in which expiration is stronger. Name the four periods of the postasphyxial state: asphyxial coma, stupor, disorientation and memory impairment, residual effects. When do subconjunctival ecchymoses appear? In the stage of dyspnoea, when arterial and venous pressure change sharply.

t: Hanging: typical and atypical types
n: Hanging: typical and atypical types. Hanging is the most frequent, 65-70%. Mostly it is a method of suicide, and accident is rare. To compress vessels and nerves the ligature need not be tightened with great force. With support on the knees the force equals 20% of body mass, and in a lying position it equals the mass of the head, 4-5 kg. Typical hanging is complete hanging, in which the body hangs freely in the ligature. Atypical hanging is incomplete: part of the body has support, and the person may be standing, sitting or lying.

t: Features of the ligature and knot
n: Features of the ligature and knot. The material of the ligature varies: soft, semi-rigid, rigid. The loop may have one, two or many turns. By movement, a sliding and a non-sliding ligature are distinguished. The knot is important criminalistically: it may indicate the professional skill of the person who made the ligature. The position of the knot is typical, that is, at the back, or atypical, that is, at the front and side. When the ligature is removed, the side opposite the knot is cut; hanging also occurs without a knot, in a universal ligature.

t: Factors of the occurrence of death in hanging
n: Factors of the occurrence of death in hanging. In hanging, death results from the combined action of several factors, and there is no single leading cause. There are four factors in all. The airway: the base of the tongue is displaced and the passage narrows. The veins are compressed and the outflow of blood from the brain is impeded. Even when the carotid arteries are compressed, blood enters through the vertebral arteries and intracranial pressure rises sharply. The reflex factor: irritation of the vagus nerve may cause cardiac arrest. With an atypical knot the oesophagus is not fully closed, so vomiting and aspiration are possible. The vertebral factor is rupture of the spinal cord in abrupt typical hanging.

t: The strangulation furrow and its classification
n: The strangulation furrow and its classification. The main sign is the strangulation furrow on the neck; it is an abrasion and depends on the properties of the ligature. The position, direction, continuity, width, depth and relief of the furrow are compared with the ligature. A rigid ligature leaves a deep furrow. If the furrow of a soft ligature is not noticeable, the “copper wire sign”, that is, Casper's sign, is found. In typical hanging the knot is at the back, and the furrow is above the hyoid bone and obliquely vertical. In atypical hanging the knot is at the front or side, the furrow may be lower, and its verticality is reduced.

t: Signs of stretching and vitality of the furrow
n: Signs of stretching and vitality of the furrow. Casper's sign: if with a soft ligature the furrow on the skin is not seen, a whitish streak is found in the internal tissues. Brouardel's sign: extensive haemorrhage in the retropharyngeal region and the posterior wall of the pharynx. There are four signs of stretching of the neck. Amussat: rupture of the intima of the carotid artery. Martin: blood in the outer coat of the carotid artery. Walcher: blood at the end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Simon: haemorrhage into the intervertebral discs. Bokarius's test and the signs of Neyding and Kasyanov confirm that the furrow was inflicted during life.

t: Ligature strangulation of the neck and the difference from hanging
n: Ligature strangulation of the neck and the difference from hanging. In ligature strangulation the reflexogenic zones are irritated more, and death may result from reflex cardiac arrest. In most cases it is homicide; injuries of struggle and self-defence may be found. Injury of the hyoid bone is not characteristic; a fracture of the horns of the thyroid cartilage is possible. In hanging the force comes from the weight of the body or part of it, the furrow is obliquely vertical and above the hyoid bone, and signs of stretching may be present. In strangulation an outside force acts, the furrow is horizontal, at the level of the thyroid cartilage or lower, and there are no signs of stretching.

t: Manual and blunt-object strangulation and positional asphyxia
n: Manual strangulation, strangulation with a blunt object, and positional asphyxia. In manual strangulation, on the neck there are round or oval bruises from the fingers, with arc-shaped abrasions from the nails over them. Internal injuries are more pronounced than external: fractures of the horns of the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage, and haemorrhages into the soft tissues. In strangulation with a blunt object, for example a stick or the back of a chair, the marks are mainly in the projection of the area of action: a bruise, abrasion, and injury of bone and cartilage. In positional asphyxia there is no furrow; a flexion fold may resemble a furrow, and the hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilages are not injured.

t: Case analysis 4: strangulation asphyxia
n: Case analysis four: strangulation asphyxia. Situation: on the neck of the corpse there is a horizontal, closed furrow of uniform width at the level of the thyroid cartilage. The signs of Amussat, Walcher and Simon were not found. Compare: in typical hanging the furrow is in the upper part of the neck, above the hyoid bone and in an obliquely vertical direction. In manual strangulation there are round or oval bruises and arc-shaped abrasions from the nails on the neck, and internal injuries are more pronounced than external. Question: to which kind is this furrow characteristic? Remember: in hanging the furrow is higher, and in strangulation it is horizontal and lower.

t: Obturation asphyxia: orifices and airways
n: Obturation asphyxia: orifices and airways. Closing the mouth and nose with a hand or soft object is a method of killing small children and weakened adults. Accidental closure occurs in an unconscious state. If there was no resistance, apart from the general asphyxial signs no characteristic ones are found; with resistance there are bruises, abrasions and haemorrhages in the gums around the mouth and nose. The airway is closed by a foreign body, loose substance, blood or vomit; most often this is an accident. Cause of death: impassability to air, spasm of the vocal cords, or reflex cardiac arrest. Attention: vomit in the airways is not always obturation. It also enters during resuscitation, transport and putrefaction, but in small amounts, and does not reach the small bronchi.

t: Drowning: true and asphyxial
n: Drowning: true and asphyxial. In true drowning water reaches the alveoli. In the asphyxial form, laryngeal spasm does not let water into the trachea and bronchi. In sea water the blood thickens, that is, hypovolaemia; pinkish-reddish spots beneath the pleura do not form. In true drowning there is persistent fine-bubbled white foam, Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots, and up to 300 ml of water is found in the stomach. In asphyxial drowning there is little foam, and it is unstable, only Tardieu's spots are present, and the stomach may contain up to 1 L of water. Attention: a Tardieu spot is not a Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spot: the latter is larger and is not found under the epicardium.

t: Methods of establishing the vitality of drowning
n: Methods of establishing the vitality of drowning. Diatom plankton are unicellular water algae with a siliceous shell; each water body has its own composition. In true drowning the plankton is found in the bone marrow and parenchymatous organs; if it is found in the lungs, it has no significance. For comparison, a 1 L water sample is taken from the water body; in asphyxial drowning the fluid at the base of the skull is examined. Pseudoplankton, particles of sand and plant dust, is identified by polarisation microscopy. In the bacteriological method, Pseudomonas putida and fluorescens confirm entry into the water during life. By the cryoscopic and other methods, freezing, refraction of light and conductivity are studied.

t: Additional findings in asphyxial drowning
n: Additional findings in asphyxial drowning. From sharp emphysema the alveolar septa are damaged, and a small amount of air passes through the pulmonary veins into the left heart: air embolism of the heart. In Suntsov's test, in asphyxial drowning it is not the right but the left ventricle that is punctured. From laryngospasm, venous hypertension arises and blood elements pass into the thoracic duct, which is lymphaemia; these signs were established by Sveshnikov and Isaev in 1986. In the cavity of the base of the skull there is 5-15 ml of fluid, which is Sveshnikov's sign. Haemorrhage into the middle and inner ear is the Ulrich-Rostoshinsky sign. Up to 1 L of water is found in the stomach.

t: Signs of a corpse's stay in water
n: Signs of a corpse's stay in water. The corpse cools quickly, the skin pales, “goose skin” appears; the body is soiled with silt and algae. Skin changes develop over time. After a few hours the skin of the fingers and toes pales and shrivels. After 2-5 days the palm takes on the look of a “washerwoman's hand”. After 5-8 days the sole is completely involved. After 2-3 weeks the skin of the palm becomes a “glove of death”. The hair is pulled out easily after 10-15 days; the speed depends on temperature, clothing and age, not on the cause of death. In reflex arrest immediately after entering the water, the signs of asphyxia do not have time to develop; this is sudden death in water.

t: Sudden death in water
n: Sudden death in water. Sometimes, immediately on entering the water, reflex arrest of the heartbeat and breathing occurs; the general signs of asphyxia do not have time to develop. This is called the reflex, that is, syncopal, type of drowning, but it is more correct to assess it as “sudden death in water”. On careful examination, changes leading to sudden death or creating a predisposition are found in the internal organs, first of all in the heart. Predisposing factors: heat stroke, severe overtiredness, overfilling of the stomach, intoxication.

t: Case analysis and quick question 3: drowning
n: Case analysis and quick question three: drowning. Case: in the airways of a body recovered from water, a small amount of gastric contents was found; none in the small bronchi and alveoli. Attention: finding vomit in the airways is not proof of obturation asphyxia. Question: by what route could this mass have entered? Answer: it enters also in cardiac massage during resuscitation, in transporting the body and in putrefaction; the amount is small. Quick question: how do true and asphyxial drowning differ? Does water reach the alveoli, or does laryngospasm prevent it?

t: Injuries on a body recovered from water
n: Injuries on a body recovered from water. On bodies recovered from a water body, injuries may be vital or inflicted after death. It is kept in mind that vital injuries may have been inflicted even before entering the water. They may be inflicted by striking the water surface or the bottom of a shallow water body, and also by parts of a boat, ship or launch. After death, injuries are inflicted by fish and aquatic animals; in a strong current, striking objects, cardiac massage and artificial respiration also leave injuries.

t: Compression asphyxia and asphyxia in a confined space
n: Compression asphyxia and asphyxia in a confined space. In compression the chest and abdomen are compressed by a blunt object; this occurs in an avalanche, a crowd crush or a building collapse. Compression of the chest alone is more dangerous than compression of the abdomen alone; frontal compression is more dangerous than lateral. Characteristic signs: the ecchymotic mask, that is, Olivier-Danger's sign, and carmine oedema of the lungs, that is, Lacassagne's sign. In a confined space oxygen falls and CO2 rises; there are no characteristic signs, and the signs of rapid death are present; examples are a well, a refrigerator, a plastic bag. Carbon dioxide leads to death at 8-10% in adults, and is dangerous at 2.0-2.5% in children.

t: Conclusion and final case analysis
n: Conclusion and final case analysis. Three types of mechanical asphyxia: from compression, from closure, and in a confined space. Compression may be strangulation or compression asphyxia proper. The general asphyxial signs, such as Tardieu's spots and fluid dark blood, are non-specific; the asphyxial heart, anaemia and a contracted spleen are relatively pathognomonic. The totality is assessed. In hanging the furrow is higher and oblique and signs of stretching, for example Amussat's, may be present; in ligature strangulation the furrow is horizontal and lower, and such signs are absent. Final question: on the neck there is a horizontal closed furrow, the horns of the thyroid cartilage are broken, and Amussat's sign is absent. Which type is likely and why?
